builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: TPCS: A Cycle-Level Simulation Paradigm with Native Execution Semantics for RTL Modeling and Generation
summary: TPCS replaces event-driven RTL simulation (e.g., Verilator) with a transaction-based intermediate abstraction that uses host CPU control flow to prune inactive logic while remaining translatable to synthesizable RTL. Its cost is adoption of a new modeling framework and toolchain rather than compute or memory, since simulation runs on a host CPU. It can fail if the evaluated traces do not represent the reader's designs, if automatic RTL generation misses corner cases requiring explicit event semantics, or if ecosystem immaturity limits integration with existing verification flows.
rationale: This is a hardware design and RTL simulation framework for pre-RTL microarchitecture exploration, which falls outside the reader's AI/ML production scope of model serving, training, or agent systems.

claims.statement: TPCS replaces event-driven RTL simulation (e.g., Verilator) with a transaction-based intermediate abstraction that uses host CPU control flow to prune inactive logic while remaining translatable to synthesizable RTL. Its cost is adoption of a new modeling framework and toolchain rather than compute or memory, since simulation runs on a host CPU. It can fail if the evaluated traces do not represent the reader's designs, if automatic RTL generation misses corner cases requiring explicit event semantics, or if ecosystem immaturity limits integration with existing verification flows.

The paper claims 36x-42x speedups over parallel Verilator on SMP systems and 3.4x-7.2x over single-threaded Verilator on accelerators, with cycle-level waveform agreement and generated RTL within -4.7% to +2.6% clock period and -3.3% to +4.0% area of handcrafted designs.
